items.title: 20.3 Comparison of Reactivity of Benzene with Alkanes and Alkenes

source_refs.note: Topic 20.3 with Quick Check 20.3, printed page 61.

blocks.text: Alkanes are generally an unreactive class of organic compounds due to their non-polar nature and the presence of sigma bond only. However, they undergo free radical substitution reactions in the presence of UV light quite easily. Alkenes, on the other hand, are very reactive class of organic compounds due to the presence of π bond and the availability of π electrons for electrophilic reagents. They undergo electrophilic addition reactions easily.

Benzene has three π bonds and, as expected, shows some similarities to alkenes in being reactive towards electrophilic species. However, there are two key differences between their reactions with electrophiles:

items: benzene is very stable and thus less reactive.
Unlike alkenes, it undergoes the electrophilic substitution and not electrophilic addition reactions:

blocks.alt: Left, electrophilic substitution: benzene with its H highlighted, Br2 over the arrow and FeBr3 under it, gives bromobenzene + HBr; the H has been replaced by the Br. Right, electrophilic addition: cyclohexene with an H on each double-bond carbon, with Br2, gives 1,2-dibromocyclohexane, each of those carbons now carrying H and Br; two Br have been added to the double bond.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic substitution of benzene and electrophilic addition to cyclohexene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 64).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed figure crosses out the arrow for cyclohexene + Br2, but cyclohexene adds bromine readily; the arrow is drawn without the cross. It is benzene that does not undergo this addition.

Bromine in the electrophilic substitution reaction replaces a hydrogen atom. This is due to the stability of the aromatic ring which is due to extensive delocalization of π electrons. Even though the reaction in benzene goes through an intermediate where the aromaticity is broken, it is restored after the completion of the reaction. Therefore, electrophilic substitution does not affect the overall stability of the benzene ring. In electrophilic addition the delocalisation is broken and addition is not favourable.

items: Although benzene is highly unsaturated yet it does not prefer to undergo addition reactions. Explain.
